notes.title: Parametric typing versus raw legacy APIs
notes.core: A raw generic type drops compile-time type checks and pushes failures to distant casts; List<?> retains read-only element-type uncertainty without permitting arbitrary insertion. A List<Object> is not a universal supertype of List<String>.
rules: Prefer parameterized types to catch wrong elements at source instead of after retrieval.
When an API accepts values of unknown element type and does not insert typed elements, a wildcard is safer than a raw type.
Only null can be inserted through a bare Collection<?> without a capture or stronger type.
Raw usage remains a legacy interoperability escape hatch, including a class literal or instanceof involving an unbounded form.
nuance: A List<Object> accepts arbitrary Objects; a List<?> can stand for any list but cannot safely accept those arbitrary values.
Some legacy interop boundaries need careful localized unchecked bridges, not pervasive raw declarations.
@SuppressWarnings does not make runtime casts safe.
notes.misconception: Replacing List<?> with List<Object> as if they were interchangeable.
notes.scene: A message-inspection API receives List<String>, List<UUID> and List<Long> but only needs to count entries.

notes.title: Unchecked-warning triage and proof obligations
notes.core: Unchecked warnings signal possible unsound casts or transfers. Remove the cause when possible, otherwise prove the operation safe and suppress only at the narrowest declaration with a specific rationale.
rules: A clean -Xlint:unchecked compilation should be a project goal.
An unchecked cast may be valid under a privately enforced invariant; document its proof, not just intent.
Prefer local variable or tiny helper-level suppression to class-wide annotations.
A suppression that hides subsequent new warnings creates a silent maintenance regression.
nuance: An unchecked cast warning is not proof that the operation fails at runtime; it is proof the compiler cannot verify it.
An Object[] backing store cast to E[] needs to stay private and prevent foreign element insertion.
Compiler-specific lint configurations affect whether warning cleanup is visible.
notes.misconception: Treating a successful -nowarn compilation as proof of type safety.
notes.scene: An adapter maps a legacy API returning List into a typed batch of payment reconciliation rows.

notes.title: Array reification and generic invariance
notes.core: Arrays carry a reified runtime component type and are covariant, so some bad stores fail at runtime; parameterized collections are invariant and mostly erased, which blocks analogous unsafe assignments at compilation.
rules: Assigning a subtype array to a supertype array can compile and still throw ArrayStoreException on insertion.
List<Integer> cannot be assigned to List<Number> because mutating the latter would compromise the former.
Generic array creation for a nonreifiable element type is prohibited; prefer List<T> or a carefully justified internal cast.
Array APIs can still be appropriate for primitives, interop or measured workloads, rather than blanket banning arrays.
nuance: An array of unbounded-wildcard lists is legal because the component type is reifiable; it is not a normal List<String>[] creation.
Array runtime stores and generic compile-time checking solve different safety problems.
A heap pollution warning is a cue to inspect varargs and unchecked bridges.
notes.misconception: Believing arrays and List have the same subtyping rules.
notes.scene: A batch parser API accepts a collection of event handlers with different concrete payload types.

notes.title: Designing reusable generic containers
notes.core: A container should expose its element type explicitly to callers, preventing client casts. Internal Object[] storage and private checked casts can sometimes support safe implementation, but external additions must honor E.
rules: Make the class generic at its API boundary so push/pop preserve the same type parameter.
Type erasure prevents new E[] directly; a private Object[] implementation can return E through a carefully isolated unchecked cast.
Clear unused array slots after pop to avoid unintentionally retaining object references.
Never expose internal storage as E[] to an unrelated caller when its runtime type cannot support that promise.
nuance: An internally used unchecked cast is safe only if all paths into storage respect E.
An ArrayList<E> delegate can avoid manual array casts at a modest different footprint.
Generic type parameters can be bounded, but bounds should express real operations required by the container.
notes.misconception: Assuming making the signature generic automatically makes an Object[] backing store safe.
notes.scene: A retry work queue holds only RetryTask values with consistent push/pop contracts.

notes.title: Generic methods and recursive bounds
notes.core: Generic methods can express relationships between arguments and result types without raw casts. A recursive bound such as T extends Comparable<? super T> describes safe comparable contracts.
rules: A generic method type parameter is declared before the return type, independent of class genericity.
A reusable immutable identity function can return its argument, preserving T without creating per-type functions.
Type inference should keep callers cast-free when their inputs agree with declared method constraints.
Recursive bounds model comparison among admissible types, not arbitrary objects.
nuance: Set union typed at E may infer a broader common type only when return expectations allow it.
An explicit type witness can occasionally guide inference, but should not become everyday noise.
An unsafe raw identity function is not equivalent to a type-safe generic method.
notes.misconception: Using Object return values where T could preserve caller types.
notes.scene: A sorting helper picks the smaller of two comparable versions in a deployment reconciler.

notes.title: Wildcard variance: producers, consumers and capture
notes.core: For generic API flexibility, a source producing E often uses ? extends E, while a destination consuming E often uses ? super E. Comparator and Comparable participate as consumers; wildcard capture sometimes needs an internal generic helper.
rules: Iterable<? extends E> can supply E-compatible values while List<? super E> can accept E values.
List<? extends Number> cannot safely accept an arbitrary Number because its true element subtype is unknown.
Comparator<? super T> allows comparators for a supertype to order T.
Avoid using wildcards in simple return types that force callers to reason about capture unless the API needs that flexibility.
nuance: PECS is a rule of thumb dependent on whether a parameter produces, consumes or both.
If the caller must place values in and read specific types out, explicit T may be better than a wildcard.
Unbounded wildcard swap may require a private generic method to capture an unknown but consistent element type.
notes.misconception: Using extends everywhere as if it means any subtype can be appended.
notes.scene: An alert delivery batch copies specialized events into a broader sink, then sorts them with a comparator of Event.

notes.title: Varargs, erased generics and safe array handling
notes.core: A parameterized varargs argument is backed by an array whose runtime type may not enforce its generic element promise. A safe varargs method neither writes incompatible array contents nor leaks that mutable array to untrusted clients.
rules: Heap pollution arises if a variable of a parameterized type points to a value that violates its declared parameterization.
@SafeVarargs is a promise by the author; the annotation suppresses warnings but does not make an unsafe body safe.
Check that a varargs method does not expose its array or store values of the wrong parameterized type.
Prefer Collection or List inputs when a varargs API complicates proof of safety.
nuance: A non-reifiable generic varargs warning is relevant even when the method signature looks type-safe.
Storing an array into a field or returning it can invalidate the non-escape proof.
Heap pollution may produce ClassCastException later in a different method, making diagnosis difficult.
notes.misconception: Adding @SafeVarargs to an arbitrary generic varargs method and treating it as a fix.
notes.scene: A batch operation aggregates Lists of event IDs and needs a safe entry point.

notes.title: Typesafe heterogeneous maps using type tokens
notes.core: When values have unrelated types, place a type parameter on a token key such as Class<T> rather than parameterizing the entire container. Use key.cast at retrieval and validate insertion when accepting untrusted raw maps.
rules: Map<Class<?>,Object> can hold heterogeneous values but a generic accessor links a Class<T> key to a T result.
Class<T>.cast checks the runtime class at lookup and can enforce key-value consistency.
Raw Class misuse can still corrupt such a map; consider checked insertion and boundary validation.
Parameterized type tokens have limits because List<String>.class does not exist under erasure.
nuance: A nonnull value may be a subtype of the key type and still pass Class.cast.
Annotation-style bounded tokens may express a bounded key space where only certain token types are valid.
Custom typed keys (e.g. Column<T>) can generalize beyond Class key identity.
notes.misconception: Believing Map<Class<?>,Object> alone enforces matching key/value types.
notes.scene: An interview grading context stores independent metadata such as Duration, Locale and AttemptId without unsafe casts at call sites.
